tagline.text: Bohol's largest coral-stone church, destroyed by an earthquake and reborn after eight years

location.label: Location
location.text: Poblacion (Moto), Loon, western Bohol, about 27–28 km north of Tagbilaran

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,500 (per person, based on a round-trip day trip from Tagbilaran by public transport including meals)

children.text: Loon Church is a coral-stone church completed in the 1860s on the site of a parish founded by the Jesuits in 1753. It was completely destroyed by the 2013 Bohol earthquake and its restoration was finished in September 2021. Together with the nearby Inang-angan stone stairway, it makes a signature heritage route in western Bohol.
Loon is a coastal town at the western end of Bohol, about
north of Tagbilaran. It sits roughly halfway between Tagbilaran and the northwestern port of Tubigon, so both are about
40 minutes
away by bus, jeepney or van. At the center of town stands the
Parish Church of Nuestra Señora de la Luz (Our Lady of Light)

, commonly known as Loon Church. Local guides describe it as the largest church on Bohol, and one source gives its floor area as about 2,245 sq m. The parish was founded by the Jesuits on June 22, 1753, and its patroness, Our Lady of Light, is known locally as "Birhen sa Kasilak."

What makes this church special is not only its age but what happened on October 15, 2013. The magnitude 7.2 Bohol earthquake brought down the church and its neighboring convent completely, and Loon was one of the towns with the most casualties. Restoration work went on for nearly eight years, and on September 7, 2021, the eve of the feast of Our Lady of Light, the restored church was handed over to the Diocese of Tagbilaran. The building you see today was rebuilt from ruins, so it carries the story of Boholanos rising from the rubble. News reports at the time of the reopening said the church had come back to something close to its original form, and the town government lists it as the first of Loon's heritage sites.

The roots of the building go back further. The first Jesuit church is said to have stood not in today's Moto but in the coastal settlement of Napo, and the town center later moved inland to Moto because of pirate raids. The 1770s complex reportedly had defensive stone walls and a cannon, and the church suffered two fires, in 1850 and 1853. Only the façade survived, and the present church, designed by Domingo de Escondrillas, the public works director of Cebu, was built with local labor between 1855 and 1864. Some sources give 1890 as the final completion date, so treat the years as approximate. In 2010 the church was declared both a National Historical Landmark and a National Cultural Treasure.

You can see it in half a day. Look at the churchyard and the interior, then walk down the coral-stone Inang-angan stairway, which starts in the alley right beside the church, to the seaside village of Napo. If time allows, add the coastal town and a view over the mangroves. If you are staying in Tagbilaran or Panglao and also visiting southern churches such as Loboc and Baclayon, this adds the western side of the church circuit in one go. Loon also lies on the way to the northern port of Tubigon, so it fits easily into trips to and from Cebu. If you have seen photos of Loon Church from before the earthquake, it is interesting to compare them with the restored building. Next to the church, a school (Sacred Heart Academy) is said to occupy the site of the old convent, so the surroundings can be noisy when students come and go. Early mornings and weekday afternoons are the calmest times in the churchyard. From the church to the stairway entrance is only a few minutes on foot through the alley beside the plaza, so the whole outing can be done on foot.

The façade is the part that survived the fires of the 1850s, and inscriptions on it are said to address Queen Isabella and the governor-general. The right-hand tower of the twin octagonal bell towers has a clock installed in
. Unlike the Loboc and Baclayon churches, which have a portico, this church has a Baroque-style façade without one.

The entrance hall has an azulejo tile floor and a ceiling painting of the "Entry into Jerusalem," and the nave has three neo-Gothic altars. The central altar holds the image of Our Lady of Light. The interior murals are said to have been painted by Raymundo Francia in 1938. Check on site for details of the interior after restoration. The octagonal mortuary chapel and the site of the old cemetery in the church grounds can reportedly be seen from the outside, but their uses have changed, so ask locally whether they are open.
This stone stairway runs from beside the church down to the seaside village of Napo. The Loon municipal guide describes four flights totaling
174 steps

, plus a fifth flight of 38 steps up to the convent, for 212 steps in all. The bottom ends near the fish port, with views of the sea, mangroves and mountains. It was also the first earthquake-damaged heritage structure in Bohol that the National Museum finished restoring, in 2016.

Napo was the old coastal center, and the ruins of the Saiz family house remain there. Loon is also known for a community theater tradition called "Drama," dating from the Spanish period, in which villagers write, direct, sing and act. Performances are not on a fixed schedule, so ask the municipal tourism office.

blocks.title: Holy Week rites and the Hugosan

children.text: In front of the church stands a four-column platform called the Hugosan, which is used in Easter rites. On Good Friday there is a pilgrimage to the cross at dawn, followed by a procession later in the day. The town is crowded during Holy Week, so go on a weekday if you want a quiet visit.
Loon's patronal feast is
September 8

, and a "Festival of Lights" (SidlaKasilak) is held in September. Because the church was handed over on the eve of the feast, this season has special meaning since the restoration. Lodging and transport get busy during feast week.
An intertidal zone of about
417 hectares

, created when the seabed was lifted by the 2013 earthquake, is protected as the Loon Coastal Geomorphic Conservation Park. At low tide you can see how the earthquake changed the landscape. Check locally how it is open to visitors.
Cabilao Island, part of Loon, is known for diving and white sand beaches, and some travelers continue there by boat after seeing the church. Boat times change with the weather.
Take a bus or van bound for Loon or Tubigon from the Dao terminal in Tagbilaran.
Get off at the Loon plaza and look at the churchyard and façade.
If Mass is not in progress, quietly look around the nave and the altars.
Walk down the Inang-angan stairway to the seaside at Napo.
Have lunch at a coastal eatery or a restaurant in town.
Climb back to the church, or take a tricycle to the plaza.
Take a bus to Tagbilaran or Tubigon.

The stairway involves going up and down, and it is hot at midday. Plan to go down in the morning and avoid climbing in the afternoon heat. During Holy Week and the September feast, roads can be congested because of events, so allow extra time.
Start from Tubigon or Tagbilaran and see Loon Church and the Inang-angan stairway.
After lunch, head toward the nearby Calape church.
Return toward Tagbilaran.
Flights run from Manila to Bohol-Panglao International Airport (TAG) and take about
1 hour 20 minutes
. Check airlines and schedules when you book.
From the airport to Tagbilaran takes about
30 minutes
by taxi or van.
The Loon town tourism guide gives about
27 km
from Tagbilaran, about
37 minutes
by bus or public transport, and lists the fare as
, but that guide is undated. Recent travel portals list about ₱100~170, so check the fare on site.
Coming from Tagbilaran, the church is on the left side of the national highway just before the Loon public plaza. Coming from Tubigon, it is on the right after the plaza.
A private vehicle takes about
25–40 minutes
and is easy to fit to your sightseeing plans.
You can also join a one-day tour that combines it with the southern churches.
The church and the entrance to the Inang-angan stairway are one alley apart. For the outskirts toward Napo, use a tricycle or motorcycle taxi.

Loon has a tropical climate on Bohol's western coast and is warm all year. Because walking is the main activity, the dry season is best, and in the rainy season frequent showers make the stairway and the road to Napo slippery. The churchyard has little shade at midday, so mornings are recommended.
Holy Week and the September feast add events to see, but they also bring crowds and a shortage of rooms.

Loon has small guesthouses and homestays, but the choice is limited. Most travelers stay in Tagbilaran or Panglao and come as a day trip, while those who want to dive stay at a resort on Cabilao Island. Book ahead for Holy Week and the September feast. The simplest plan is to see the church and be back in Tagbilaran before dark. Public transport thins out late in the day, so ask about the last departure in the morning.

Food centers on restaurants and the market in town. Loon is known for binago, a cassava snack, tubâ, a coconut toddy, and handicrafts such as woven mats and baskets. Some village eateries close early, so have lunch promptly. Coconut drinks and cassava snacks sold on the street are a nice way to rest after the stairway.
The church is a place of worship, so dress with shoulders and knees covered and stay quiet during Mass.
The Inang-angan stairway goes up and down, so bring comfortable shoes and water.
It is easier to go down in the morning and come back up when the sun is weaker.
Check on-site rules for photography inside, and do not disturb worshippers near the altar.
The church and the stairway are close together, so see them in one visit.
Tell the conductor ahead of time that you are getting off at "Loon Church."
Bring enough cash. Many small-town places do not accept cards.
Combine Loon with Tubigon or Calape in a single day to make the travel efficient.

The inscriptions on the façade and the clock on the twin bell tower are more interesting up close. Walk slowly around the churchyard to look at them, and choose your photo time by watching the direction of the light yourself.
The church is a working parish, so viewing may be restricted during Mass and events. Check local notices for opening hours and interior rules after the restoration.
The number of steps and the construction dates differ between sources, so figures may vary slightly.
Bus fares and times change, so check the latest information.
The stairway and the road to Napo are slippery on rainy days.
Boats to Cabilao Island can be canceled depending on the weather.

, part of Loon, is a small island known for diving. You cross by boat.
